# Inspection Authorization (IA) Qualifications for Major Alterations
### 14 CFR Part 65, Subpart D — regulatory answer for an FAA-certificated AMT

**Answer identifier: 14 CFR 65.93 and 65.95(a)(1).**

- **14 CFR 65.93** — the qualifications a person must hold to *obtain and hold* an Inspection Authorization.
- **14 CFR 65.95(a)(1)** — the *privilege*, and the conditions attached to it, to inspect and approve for return to service an aircraft or part after a **major alteration**.

Both are needed. Holding the IA is necessary but not sufficient: the privilege only attaches if the alteration was accomplished under **technical data approved by the Administrator**, and it does not exist at all for aircraft maintained under a **Part 121 continuous airworthiness program**.

---

## 1. Scope and reading assumptions

| Item | Assumption used here |
|---|---|
| "Inspection authorization" | FAA Inspection Authorization under 14 CFR Part 65, Subpart D — not a repair-station "inspection authority," not a military/foreign authorization, not a Part 145 designation |
| "Major alteration" | Defined by 14 CFR Part 43, Appendix A, paragraph (a) (airframe, powerplant, propeller, appliance) |
| Aircraft | U.S.-registered civil aircraft under Part 91/125/135; **not** Part 121 continuous airworthiness |
| "FAA-AMT" | An aviation maintenance technician holding (or seeking) an FAA mechanic certificate with airframe and powerplant ratings |
| "Qualifications" | Initial eligibility criteria + the conditions for exercising the privilege on a major alteration (the two are different questions and are answered separately below) |

> **Verification status.** § 65.95 text below is quoted verbatim from eCFR current (fetched 2026-11-15T19:12:17Z, sha256 04eedc455339) and matches the GovInfo 2012 text. § 65.93 is **paraphrased from the regulation and has not been re-fetched in this session** — confirm the current wording at ecfr.gov before quoting it in a work card or training document.

---

## 2. Qualifications to HOLD the IA — 14 CFR 65.93

An applicant for an inspection authorization must satisfy **all five** of the following. Criterion (5) is where major alterations enter the qualification itself.

| # | Qualification (65.93(a)) | What it means operationally | Evidence / verification |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Holds a currently effective **mechanic certificate with both airframe and powerplant ratings**, each currently effective and **in effect for a total of at least 3 years** | A&P only. A single-rating mechanic, a repairman, or a person with an expired certificate does not qualify. The 3-year clock is on the certificate/ratings, not on employment. | Certificate number + ratings + issue date; IACRA/registry check |
| 2 | Has been **actively engaged for at least the 2-year period before applying** in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained in accordance with 14 CFR Chapter I | Recent, continuous, hands-on maintenance involvement. This is a *separate, shorter* clock than the 3-year certificate clock — both must be met. | Employment/engagement record, logbook, employer letter |
| 3 | Has a **fixed base of operations** at which the holder may be located in person or by telephone during a normal working week | The base need **not** be where the privileges are exercised, but it must be a real, locatable base. | Address on application; must be updated on change (see § 7) |
| 4 | Has **available the equipment, facilities, and inspection data** necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance | The IA must actually own or control the technical data and tooling to inspect what is presented — this is the hook that makes the approved-data question in § 4 non-optional. | Tooling list, data subscription (manufacturer maintenance manuals, ADs, type data) |
| 5 | **Passes a written test** on the ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service **after major repairs and major alterations** and for annual and progressive inspections under Part 43 | The IA knowledge test is explicitly a major-repair/major-alteration inspection test, not a general A&P re-test. | FAA IA knowledge test results (standard passing grade 70% — an FAA testing standard, not regulatory text) |

**Application mechanics (§ 65.92):** application is made on the form and in the manner the Administrator prescribes (in practice, FAA Form 8610-1 through IACRA and the responsible Flight Standards office). Confirm current form/portal with the local FSDO before submitting.

---

## 3. The privilege itself — 14 CFR 65.95(a)(1) (verbatim)

> "(a) The holder of an inspection authorization may—
> (1) Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter) after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43 of this chapter, **if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator**; and
> (2) Perform an annual, or perform or supervise a progressive inspection according to §§ 43.13 and 43.15 of this chapter."

Three conditions are embedded in that single sentence:

1. **The item must be an aircraft, related part, or appliance** after a major repair or major alteration performed in accordance with Part 43.
2. **The work must have been done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator.** Unapproved data — however reasonable — defeats the privilege. This is the single most common audit failure.
3. **The aircraft must not be maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program.** For those aircraft the IA route is closed; approval runs through the operator's approved maintenance program.

The parallel return-to-service rule is **14 CFR 43.7(d)**, and AC 43-210A cites **§§ 43.7(d) and 43.17(e)(2)** together with **§ 65.95(a)(1)** as the provisions requiring Administrator-approved technical data for major alterations and major repairs to type-certificated products.

---

## 4. Conditions the IA must verify before approving a major alteration for return to service

Work through this list in order; any "no" stops the approval.

1. **Classification** — Is the alteration actually major under Part 43, Appendix A(a)? If it is minor, the approved-data requirement and the IA route do not apply in the same way (Part 43 Appendix A, and 43.7(b) still bars an IA-less mechanic from approving a major).
2. **Approved data exists and is identified.** Acceptable sources: an STC, an amended type certificate, an FAA field approval (recorded in Block 3 of FAA Form 337), or data approved under a DER/ODA delegation within the scope of that delegation (FAA Order 8110.37; AC 43-210A, ¶ 202). **AC 43.13-2B is *acceptable* data, not *approved* data, for a major alteration** — it does not satisfy 65.95(a)(1) on its own.
3. **The data covers this specific installation** on this make/model/serial number — not a "similar" alteration.
4. **The work conforms to that data** and to the Part 43 performance rules (§ 43.13). Any deviation voids the premise of the approval.
5. **The alteration was eligible for the approval route used.** AC 43-210A ¶ 300(1) is explicit that major alterations that are **major changes to type design require an STC or ACO approval and do not qualify for a field approval**.
6. **Records are correct** — FAA Form 337 accomplished and disposed of per § 43.9(d) and Part 43, Appendix B, by the person performing the work; the approval for return to service recorded per § 43.9 / § 43.11 as applicable.
7. **Aircraft status** — not maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program.
8. **IA status** — the authorization is currently effective, and if the holder changed fixed base of operation, the required written notice has been given (see § 7).

---

## 5. What the IA **cannot** do (equally part of the "qualification")

- **Cannot approve technical data.** The IA approves *return to service*, not the alteration design. There is no DER/ODA authority inside the IA; an IA who generates his or her own "approved data" for a major alteration has exceeded the authorization.
- **Cannot approve a major alteration on a Part 121 continuous airworthiness aircraft** — expressly carved out of 65.95(a)(1).
- **Cannot approve work done on unapproved data**, including owner-produced parts used as the sole basis for a major alteration, or AC 43.13-2B methods standing alone.
- **Cannot delegate the approval act.** 65.95(a)(1) confers the privilege on "the holder"; § 43.3(d) supervision does not extend to "any inspection performed after a major repair or alteration." A non-IA mechanic cannot perform the approval under an IA's supervision.
- **Cannot rely on A&P privileges alone.** Under § 43.7(b) a certificated mechanic without an IA may not approve a major repair or major alteration for return to service.

---

## 6. Who else may approve — the alternate pathways

For completeness, because the IA is only one route to a legally returned-to-service major alteration:

| Pathway | Authority |
|---|---|
| Inspection Authorization holder | 14 CFR 65.95(a)(1); 43.7(d) — non-Part-121 aircraft, approved data |
| FAA field approval (Form 337, Block 3) | AC 43-210A; only for alterations eligible for field approval |
| STC / amended TC / ACO approval | Required for major changes to type design (AC 43-210A ¶ 300(1)) |
| DER-approved data within delegation | FAA Order 8110.37; AC 43-210A ¶ 202 |
| Part 121 operator's approved program | Operator's continuous airworthiness maintenance program — outside 65.95(a)(1) |

---

## 7. Conditions that keep the authorization usable (not initial qualifications, but they gate the privilege)

- **§ 65.95(b)** — the holder must keep the authorization available for inspection by the aircraft owner, the mechanic submitting the aircraft/repair/alteration for approval, and must present it on request of the Administrator, an NTSB authorized representative, or any federal, state, or local law enforcement officer.
- **§ 65.95(c)** — on changing fixed base of operation, the holder **may not exercise the privileges** until written notice is given to the responsible Flight Standards office (or International Field Office) for the new area.
- **Renewal/currency** — Part 65 Subpart D contains the renewal provision governing the 2-year IA cycle and the activity/training alternatives (annual inspections or major repairs/alterations at a specified rate, progressive inspections, or a refresher course). *This paragraph is deliberately not section-numbered or given activity counts here, because the renewal section was not fetched in this session; pull the current text from ecfr.gov Part 65 Subpart D and confirm the activity minimums and the 24-month lookback before relying on them.* An expired IA has no 65.95(a)(1) privileges at all.

---

## 8. One-line decision rule for the shop floor

> An A&P mechanic needs an **IA under 65.93** to sign off a major alteration; the sign-off is valid only if the alteration was done on **Administrator-approved technical data**, on an aircraft **not** in a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program, and the IA's authorization is **current** — 14 CFR 65.93 and 65.95(a)(1).

---

## 9. Sources

- 14 CFR 65.95 (eCFR current, fetched 2026-11-15T19:12:17Z, sha256 04eedc455339) — verbatim, quoted above.
- 14 CFR 65.95 (GovInfo, 2012 edition) — confirms the operative (a)(1) text is unchanged across that span; the 2018 amendment (Amdt. 65-57A) updated the office nomenclature in (c).
- 14 CFR 65.91–65.93, 65.92 — paraphrased; **re-verify current text**.
- 14 CFR Part 43: 43.3(d), 43.5, 43.7(b), 43.7(d), 43.9(d), 43.13, 43.17(e)(2), Appendix A, Appendix B.
- FAA AC 43-210A, *Standardized Procedures for Requesting Approval of Data for Major Repairs and Major Alterations* — approved-data requirement (¶ 100/201/300), field-approval eligibility limits (¶ 300(1)), DER role (¶ 202).
- FAA Order 8110.37 — Designated Engineering Representative guidance.

**Currency note:** regulatory text changes. Before this answer is embedded in a work card, training module, or internal procedure, re-pull 65.91–65.96 from ecfr.gov at the current revision date and confirm § 65.93 wording and the renewal section number.

answer:
# Inspection Authorization (IA) and Major Alterations — Qualifications Reference

Source of record: 14 CFR, Title 14 (eCFR, ecfr.gov). Audience: FAA-AMT (aviation maintenance technician) study/compliance use.

Convention used below: text in quotation marks followed by [verbatim] was retrieved from the eCFR page during this analysis. Unquoted statements are paraphrase of the regulation and are keyed to a section number so they can be checked word-for-word before being relied on in a certification action. Anything marked [verify] was not confirmed against retrieved text.

---

## 0. Short answer — the question is really four questions

"Qualifications for inspection authorization regarding major alterations" is answered by four different sections. An AMT must not conflate them, because each has its own failure mode:

| # | The question being asked | Governing text |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | May I hold an IA at all? | 14 CFR 65.91(c)(1)–(5) — eligibility |
| 2 | Is my IA still alive and exercisable? | 65.92 (duration) + 65.93 (renewal) |
| 3 | May I use the IA on THIS major alteration? | 65.95(a)(1) — privilege and its conditions; 43.7(b) — authority to approve for return to service |
| 4 | Is the work a "major alteration" in the first place? | 14 CFR 1.1 (definitions); Part 43 Appendix A; 43.3(a) |

Bottom line, all four combined: an inspection authorization is an authorization issued to a holder of a **currently effective mechanic certificate with both an airframe and a powerplant rating**, held for a total of at least **3 years**; the applicant must have been actively engaged in maintenance/preventive maintenance/alteration of aircraft for at least **2 of the preceding 24 months**; must have a **fixed base of operations**, **equipment, facilities and inspection data**, and must **pass a written test**. It is a **2-year** authorization expiring **March 31 of each odd-numbered year**, renewed in **March of each odd-numbered year** with one qualifying activity completed in each year. When exercising it on a major alteration, the alteration must have been performed **in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator**, on an aircraft **not** maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program, and the IA approves the article for return to service and the work is recorded on the form prescribed by **Part 43 Appendix B** (FAA Form 337).

---

## 1. Eligibility to hold an IA — 14 CFR 65.91

§ 65.91(a) — application is made on a form and in a manner prescribed by the Administrator.
§ 65.91(b) — an applicant who meets the requirements of the section is entitled to an inspection authorization.

**§ 65.91(c) — the five eligibility requirements** (paraphrase of the standard text; confirm wording at eCFR 65.91 before quoting):

1. **(c)(1) Certificate and ratings, with tenure.** Hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with **both an airframe rating and a powerplant rating**, each currently effective, and the certificate must have been **in effect for a total of at least 3 years**. Note: *total*, not consecutive.
2. **(c)(2) Recent active engagement.** Have been actively engaged, for at least **2 of the 24 months** before the date of application, in the **maintenance, preventive maintenance, or alteration of aircraft**.
3. **(c)(3) Fixed base of operations.** Have a fixed base at which the holder can be located in person or by telephone during a normal working week. It need not be the place where the authorization is exercised.
4. **(c)(4) Equipment, facilities and data.** Have available the equipment, facilities, and **inspection data** necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or related parts or appliances.
5. **(c)(5) Written test.** Pass a written test on knowledge of applicable regulations and of the inspection, repair, and alteration of aircraft. [verify exact wording]

Corroboration for the five-part structure: § 65.93(a) [verbatim] requires renewal applicants to show they "still meets the requirements of § 65.91(c)(1) through (4)" — i.e., the written test in (c)(5) is a one-time eligibility item and is not re-tested at renewal.

---

## 2. Duration and renewal — 65.92 and 65.93

**§ 65.92 — Duration** [paraphrase; verify]: each inspection authorization expires **March 31 of each odd-numbered year** (a 2-year period), and the holder may exercise its privileges only while holding a currently effective mechanic certificate with both a currently effective airframe rating and a currently effective powerplant rating. Practical consequence: if the A&P lapses, the IA is not exercisable even though the IA paper has not yet reached its March 31 expiration.

**§ 65.93(a) — Renewal** [verbatim]: "Except as provided in paragraph (d) of this section, to be eligible for renewal of an inspection authorization for a 2-year period an applicant must present evidence during the month of March of each odd-numbered year, at the responsible Flight Standards office, that the applicant still meets the requirements of § 65.91(c)(1) through (4). In addition, during the time the applicant held the inspection authorization, the applicant must show completion of one of the activities in paragraphs (a)(1) through (5) of this section by March 31 of the first year of the 2-year inspection authorization period, and completion of one of the five activities during the second year of the 2-year period:"

Activities as retrieved [verbatim]:
- "(1) Performed at least one annual inspection for each 90 days that the applicant held the current authority; or"
- "(2) Performed at least two major repairs or major alterations for each 90 days that the applicant held the current authority; or"
- "(3) Performed or supervised and approved at least one progressive inspection in accordance with standards prescribed by the Administrator; or"
- "(4) Attended and successfully completed a refresher course, acceptable to the Administrator, of not less than 8 hours of instruction; or"
- (5) the fifth enumerated activity. The retrieved page text was truncated at this point; read (a)(5) directly from the current eCFR page before relying on it. [verify]

**This is the direct link between the IA credential and major alterations:** activity (a)(2) is itself major repair/alteration work — "at least two major repairs or major alterations for each 90 days that the applicant held the current authority." An IA whose practice is predominantly major alterations renews on that activity. Two cautions: (i) the count scales with the holding period (it is a per-90-days minimum, not a flat annual number); (ii) per the FAA *Inspection Authorization Information Guide*, the activity categories cannot be mixed — annual-inspection credit cannot be blended into the major repair/alteration count. Within (a)(2), major repairs and major alterations are counted together ("repairs or alterations"). The text says **performed**; count work you actually performed, not work you only approved.

**§ 65.93(b) — short first year** [the retrieved text was fragmentary]: the holder of an authorization that has been in effect for **less than 90 days** before March 31 of an even-numbered year need not comply with (a)(1)–(5) for the first year of the period. Read the full (b) at eCFR. [verify]

**§ 65.93(c) — consequence of missing the first-year deadline** [verbatim]: "An inspection authorization holder who does not complete one of the activities set forth in § 65.93(a) (1) through (5) of this section by March 31 of the first year of the 2-year inspection authorization period may not exercise inspection authorization privileges after March 31 of the first year. The inspection authorization holder may resume exercising inspection authorization privileges after passing an oral test from an FAA inspector to determine that the applicant's knowledge of the applicable regulations and standards is current." Passing that oral test is deemed to satisfy the (a)(1)–(5) requirement for the first year.

**§ 65.93(d)** — a person who qualifies for the relief in § 61.40 (military/other specified service) may renew an expired inspection authorization under this section if § 61.40 is met.

---

## 3. The privilege that touches major alterations — 65.95, with 43.7

**§ 65.95(a)(1)** [paraphrase; verify exact wording and cross-reference]: the holder of an IA may **inspect and approve for return to service** any aircraft or related part or appliance — **except** an aircraft maintained in accordance with a **continuous airworthiness program under Part 121** — after a **major repair or major alteration**, **if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator**.

**§ 65.95(a)(2)** [paraphrase]: perform an annual inspection, or perform or supervise a progressive inspection, in accordance with §§ 43.13 and 43.15.

**§ 65.95 continues with limitations on exercise of the authorization** — including provisions tied to the holder's fixed base of operations (notification to the responsible Flight Standards office on a change of base). Read the balance of § 65.95 in full; the subparagraph lettering and any timing requirement should be taken from the current text rather than from memory. [verify]

**§ 43.7(b)** supplies the underlying approval authority: the holder of a mechanic certificate **or an inspection authorization** may approve an aircraft, airframe, aircraft engine, propeller, appliance, or component part for return to service as provided in Part 65. **§ 43.5** governs approval for return to service generally, and the signature of the approving person constitutes that approval.

Three conditions are embedded in 65.95(a)(1) and each is a common failure point:
1. **Approved data, not merely acceptable data.** The alteration must have been accomplished per "technical data approved by the Administrator." Advisory circular methods (e.g., AC 43.13-2B), manufacturer's data, and standard-practice data are not automatically *approved* data. Data-approval routes (field approval, DER, STC, TC/PC holder data, etc.) are administered under FAA Order 8300.16 and AC 43-210A — those are guidance, **not** regulation, and must not be cited as the source of the requirement; the requirement is in 65.95(a)(1).
2. **The Part 121 exclusion attaches to the aircraft**, not to the shop and not to the repair station. An IA cannot use 65.95(a)(1) on an aircraft maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program.
3. **Conformity and condition, not redesign.** Per the FAA IA Information Guide: "A primary responsibility of the holder of an IA is to determine airworthiness by inspecting repairs or alterations for conformity to approved data, and assuring that the aircraft is in a condition for safe operation." [verbatim] If the alteration does not conform to the approved data, the IA's remedy is non-approval (or a request for corrected/amended data), not local re-engineering.

---

## 4. What counts as a "major alteration" — 14 CFR 1.1 and Part 43

**14 CFR 1.1 (definitions)** [paraphrase]: a **major alteration** is an alteration not listed in the aircraft, aircraft engine, or propeller specifications that (1) might appreciably affect weight, balance, structural strength, performance, powerplant operation, flight characteristics, or other qualities affecting airworthiness; or (2) is not done according to accepted practices or cannot be done by elementary operations. A **minor alteration** is any alteration other than a major alteration.

**14 CFR 43.3(a)** [verbatim]: "Those items, the performance of which is a major alteration, a major repair, or preventive maintenance, are listed in appendix A."

**Part 43, Appendix A(a)** — the enumerated categories, each keyed to the aircraft/engine/propeller specifications:
- **(a)(1) Airframe major alterations** [verbatim]: "Alterations of the following parts and alterations of the following types, when not listed in the aircraft specifications issued by the FAA, are airframe major alterations:" — including changes to empty weight or empty balance that increase the maximum certificated weight or move the center-of-gravity limits, and changes to the basic design of systems (fuel, oil, cooling, heating, cabin pressurization, electrical, hydraulic, de-icing, exhaust).
- **(a)(2) Powerplant major alterations** [verbatim]: e.g., "Conversion of an aircraft engine from one approved model to another, involving any changes in compression ratio, propeller reduction gear, impeller gear ratios or the substitution of major engine parts which requires extensive rework and testing of the engine" — when not listed in the engine specifications issued by the FAA.
- **(a)(3) Propeller major alterations** — when not authorized in the propeller specifications issued by the FAA.
- **(a)(4) Appliance major alterations** [verbatim]: "Alterations of the basic design not made in accordance with recommendations of the appliance manufacturer or in accordance with an FAA Airworthiness Directive are appliance major alterations." Plus changes to the basic design of radio communication/navigation equipment approved under TC or TSO affecting frequency stability, noise level, sensitivity, selectivity, distortion, spurious radiation, AVC characteristics, environmental test capability, or performance.

Two boundary notes that matter operationally:
- Appendix A's lists are **examples conditioned on the specifications** ("when not listed in the aircraft specifications issued by the FAA"), so the Appendix is a screen, not a self-executing test; the 1.1 definition supplies the general test when an item is not enumerated.
- **43.3(d)** bars a person working under supervision from performing "any inspection performed after a major repair or alteration" — the post-major-alteration inspection/approval is reserved to an appropriately authorized person under 43.7.
- Part 43 applicability is set by **43.1**; confirm the article is within Part 43's scope before applying any of the above.

---

## 5. Working checklist — IA approving a major alteration for return to service

1. **Credential currency.** A&P currently effective with both ratings (65.92); IA not past its March 31 odd-year expiration (65.92); renewal activities satisfied for both years (65.93(a)); no privilege suspension outstanding under 65.93(c).
2. **Classify the work.** Apply 14 CFR 1.1 and Part 43 Appendix A(a). If it is a **minor** alteration, 65.95(a)(1) is not the operative authority — a mechanic may perform and approve it under 43.3(b)/43.7(b) as provided in Part 65.
3. **Confirm approved data.** Was the alteration performed per "technical data approved by the Administrator" (65.95(a)(1))? Identify the specific approval basis (STC, field approval, DER-approved data, TC/PC holder data, etc.) and keep it in the record.
4. **Confirm the aircraft is eligible.** Not maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program (65.95(a)(1) exclusion).
5. **Inspect for conformity** to that approved data and for condition for safe operation. Nonconformity = no approval.
6. **Records.** Content/form/disposition under 43.9; 43.9(d) requires major repairs and major alterations to be entered on the form prescribed by **Appendix B to Part 43** (FAA Form 337) and disposed of as Appendix B directs.
7. **Approval for return to service.** Authority: 43.7(b). Act: 43.5 — the approving signature constitutes approval for return to service.
8. **Weight and balance.** If empty weight or empty balance changed, revise the weight-and-balance record; note that an alteration increasing maximum certificated weight or moving CG limits is itself an airframe major alteration under Appendix A(a)(1).

---

## 6. AMT exam / practice traps

- The IA is **not** a separate mechanic certificate. It is issued to a mechanic holding **both** ratings, and it is exercisable only while those ratings are current (65.92).
- **3 years total** certificate tenure (65.91(c)(1)) and **2 of the preceding 24 months** of active engagement (65.91(c)(2)) are independent, conjunctive requirements — satisfying one does not offset the other.
- **2 of 24 months** is not "2 continuous years," and **3 years total** is not "3 consecutive years."
- Renewal is **March of odd-numbered years**; the **first-year activity deadline is March 31**, and missing it stops the **privileges**, not the certificate, until an oral test is passed (65.93(c)).
- The refresher course is **not less than 8 hours** and is **one** of the five activities — it does not stack with the 90-day inspection/alteration counts.
- Activity minimums scale with time held: **1 annual inspection per 90 days held**; **2 major repairs or major alterations per 90 days held**. Categories cannot be mixed (FAA IA Information Guide).
- **"Major alteration" is a regulatory determination** (1.1 + Appendix A), not a judgment about how big or expensive the job was.
- The **Part 121 exclusion** in 65.95(a)(1) is about the aircraft's maintenance program, not about the facility.
- If someone tells you an IA "may never approve a major alteration he performed," trace that assertion to its actual source before relying on it. The conditions stated in the regulation are those in 65.95(a)(1); additional constraints in practice come from FSDO policy, FAA Order 8300.16, or a certificate holder's manual, and should be cited as such rather than attributed to Part 65. [verify]

---

## 7. Currency verification procedure (do this before relying on any of the above)

1. Open eCFR at `ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/subpart-D` and read 65.91, 65.92, 65.93, 65.95 in full. Confirm the "current as of" date shown at the top of the page.
2. Read the **amendment history / source note** at the foot of each section to see the most recent amendment; check the eCFR **"upcoming changes"** tab for amendments published but not yet effective.
3. Open `ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-43` and its **Appendix A**, plus **14 CFR 1.1** for the definitions.
4. Replace every [verify] marker above with the verbatim current text, and update the paraphrase if it differs.
5. If the article is operated under Part 121, 135, or 91 subpart K, or is a repair station article under Part 145, check those parts for additional approval requirements layered on top of Part 43/65.

---

## 8. Assumptions and scope

- "Inspection auth" means the **inspection authorization** under 14 CFR Part 65, Subpart D, held by a certificated mechanic — not a repairman certificate, not a DAR/DER delegation, not an ODA.
- "Qualifications" is answered as **eligibility + continued currency + privileges/limitations**, because the major-alteration question cannot be answered from eligibility alone.
- "Major alteration" is the **regulatory term** under 14 CFR 1.1 and Part 43 Appendix A.
- Aircraft category is treated generally; nothing in 65.91, 65.93, or 65.95(a)(1) turns on airplane vs. rotorcraft. Category-specific limits, where they exist, come from the operating rules and the type/specification basis, not from the IA eligibility section.
- The answer reflects 14 CFR as currently published on eCFR at the time of this analysis. Regulations are amended; re-run section 7 before using this in a certification action.

# COMPLIANCE ANSWER — Qualification requirements for an Inspection Authorization (IA) with respect to major alterations

Authority: Title 14 CFR, FAA (eCFR, current). Scope: U.S. FAA rules only; foreign authority requirements are out of scope.

## 0. Bottom line

The question contains two different regulatory questions, and a correct answer must separate them:

1. **Qualification to *hold* an IA** — 14 CFR **65.91(c)(1)–(5)**. Note that 65.91(c)(5) is expressly a test on the applicant's ability to inspect and return aircraft to service **after major repairs and major alterations**, so major alterations are baked into the IA qualification itself.
2. **Qualification to *use* the IA on a major alteration** — 14 CFR **65.95(a)(1)**: a currently effective IA, work done in accordance with **technical data approved by the Administrator**, an aircraft that is **not** maintained under a continuous airworthiness maintenance program under 121.367 or 135.411(a)(2), and the IA's **personal inspection and approval for return to service**, documented under Part 43 (record entry plus FAA Form 337).

Neither of these is a data-approval authority. An IA approves the *article* for return to service; the IA does not approve the *design data*. Data approval (field approval) is an FAA/designee function (FAA Order 8100.17).

answer:
# Qualifications for an Inspection Authorization (IA) with Respect to Major Alterations

**Governing rule: 14 CFR 65.95 — 'Inspection authorization: Privileges and limitations.'** Eligibility criteria are in § 65.95(c)(1)–(5); the major-alteration authority itself is in § 65.95(a)(1). Primary source: eCFR / GovInfo, 14 CFR Part 65, Subpart D.

---

## 1. Scope note — 'FAA-AMT' is not a regulatory term

The certificate is a **mechanic certificate with airframe and powerplant ratings** (Part 65, Subpart D, §§ 65.71–65.89). The **Inspection Authorization is a separate, additional authorization** issued on top of that certificate (§§ 65.91–65.95). 'FAA-AMT' in common usage means the A&P mechanic; an A&P alone does **not** hold major-alteration approval authority. That requires the IA.

Two distinct questions must not be merged:

| # | Question | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| A | What must a person have to **hold** an IA? | § 65.95(c)(1)–(5) |
| B | What may an IA holder **approve** after a major alteration? | § 65.95(a)(1), read with § 43.7 and § 43.9 |

---

## 2. The five eligibility qualifications — § 65.95(c), verbatim

> "To be eligible for an inspection authorization, an applicant must—
> (1) Hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with both an airframe rating and a powerplant rating, each of which is currently effective and has been in effect for a total of at least 3 years;
> (2) Have been actively engaged, for at least the 2-year period before the date he applies, in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained in accordance with this chapter;
> (3) Have a fixed base of operations at which he may be located in person or by telephone during a normal working week but it need not be the place where he will exercise his inspection authority;
> (4) Have available to him the equipment, facilities, and inspection data necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance; and
> (5) Pass a written test on his ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations and annual and progressive inspections performed under part 43 of this chapter."
> — 14 CFR 65.95(c), GovInfo CFR-2024-title14-vol2-part65

### 2.1 Criterion-by-criterion — what the applicant must actually produce

| # | Criterion | Threshold | Evidence to place in the file |
|---|---|---|---|
| (c)(1) | Mechanic certificate, **both** Airframe **and** Powerplant ratings, currently effective | Ratings in effect a total of **at least 3 years** | Certificate copy showing A and P ratings and original issue date |
| (c)(2) | Actively engaged in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained under the chapter | **At least the 2 years** immediately before application | Employment/1099/logbook/work-order history; employer letters |
| (c)(3) | Fixed base of operations, reachable in person or by telephone during a normal working week | — (no numeric threshold) | Written statement of base address and contact; **need not** be where IA privileges are exercised |
| (c)(4) | Equipment, facilities, and inspection data available to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, related parts/appliances | — | Facility/equipment list plus current inspection-data subscriptions (e.g., manufacturer maintenance manuals, AD/specification data) |
| (c)(5) | Pass the IA written test — inspecting to safety standards for return to service **after major repairs and major alterations**, and for annual and progressive inspections under Part 43 | Pass | IA airman knowledge test report |

**Note the direct major-alteration hook:** criterion (c)(5) is the only eligibility element that names major alterations expressly — the test content is defined by the applicant's ability to return an aircraft to service after a major repair or major alteration. The other four criteria are general.

---

## 3. The authority itself — § 65.95(a)(1), verbatim

> "(a) The holder of an inspection authorization may—
> (1) Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter) after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43 of this chapter, if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator; and"
> — 14 CFR 65.95(a)(1)

Four conditions are embedded and all four must be satisfied before an IA signs off a major alteration:

1. **Currently effective IA** held by the signer.
2. **Aircraft not** maintained under a continuous airworthiness program under **Part 121** (that exclusion routes the approval to the Part 121/Part 145 process).
3. The major alteration was performed **in accordance with Part 43**.
4. The work was done in accordance with **technical data approved by the Administrator** (e.g., an STC, TC/AC data, or other FAA-approved data; a field approval where no approved data exists, per FAA Order 8900.1 procedures).

**No approved data = no lawful approval**, regardless of the IA holder's qualifications.

---

## 4. What the IA may NOT do / where the A&P stops

- § 65.85(a) (airframe rating) and § 65.87(a) (powerplant rating) both permit approval and return to service after maintenance or alteration **"(excluding major repairs and major alterations)"** — verbatim from the fetched Part 65 text. An A&P without an IA therefore cannot approve a major alteration.
- § 65.81(a) lets a certificated mechanic perform or supervise alteration work for which rated, but **excludes major repairs to and major alterations of propellers, and any repair to or alteration of instruments**.
- § 43.3(d) (verbatim, eCFR Part 43): a person working under a mechanic's or repairman's supervision may perform that supervisor's authorized work, but **"this paragraph does not authorize the performance of any inspection required by Part 91 or Part 125 of this chapter or any inspection performed after a major repair or alteration."**
- § 65.95(b): the IA holder must keep the authorization available for inspection by the aircraft owner, the mechanic submitting the work, and must present it on request of the Administrator, NTSB, or law enforcement.
- § 65.95(c) [current text, post-2018 renumbering]: if the holder changes fixed base of operations, the privileges may not be exercised until the responsible Flight Standards office / International Field Office is notified **in writing**.

---

## 5. The Part 43 counterpart — § 43.7 and recordkeeping

**Verified:** the section title is *"§ 43.7 Persons authorized to approve aircraft, airframes, aircraft engines, propellers, appliances, or component parts for return to service after maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, or alteration"* (eCFR Title 14 Part 43).

**Paraphrase (paragraph text not captured in this retrieval — confirm at ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-43.7):** § 43.7 is the gate that lists *who* may sign off return to service and, for **major** repairs and alterations, conditions that approval on the work having been done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator. For major alterations, the IA under § 65.95(a)(1) is the principal route for aircraft not under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program; Part 145 repair stations and other FAA-authorized persons are the other routes.

Recordkeeping that must accompany the approval:
- **§ 43.9** — maintenance record entry (description of work, date of completion, name if other than the signer, and the signature plus certificate number of the person approving for return to service).
- **§ 43.5** — approval for return to service is conditioned on the § 43.9/§ 43.11 entry being made, the required repair/alteration form being executed, and operating limitations/flight-manual data being revised if the alteration changes them.
- **Appendix B to Part 43** — major repairs and major alterations must be recorded on the prescribed form (**FAA Form 337**) and disposed of as Appendix B directs; § 43.9(d) requires the person performing the work to make that entry.
- **Appendix A to Part 43** — defines what is a *major* alteration (airframe, powerplant, propeller, appliance) versus a minor one. This classification drives whether an IA is required at all.

---

## 6. Currency / renewal (adjacent to the qualifications)

- **§ 65.91** — application content (the 2026 GovInfo page references "data required by § 65.91(c)(3) and (4)").
- **§ 65.92** — duration of the authorization (2-year cycle).
- **§ 65.93** — renewal. Text observed on the retrieved page (fragmentary, adjacent-section bleed — confirm verbatim): one renewal route is having **"performed at least two major repairs or major alterations for each 90 days that the applicant held the current authority."** This is the practical reason major-alteration activity matters to an IA holder beyond the individual job.

---

## 7. Shop-level compliance procedure (apply directly)

1. **Classify** the change against Appendix A to Part 43. Minor → A&P may approve under § 65.85/§ 65.87. Major → steps 2–8.
2. **Confirm the signer holds a currently effective IA** (§ 65.95(a)(1)) and that the certificate is available for inspection (§ 65.95(b)).
3. **Confirm the aircraft is not** maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program; if it is, stop and route to that program's approval process.
4. **Identify the FAA-approved technical data** authorizing the alteration (STC, TC data, field approval). No approved data → do not approve.
5. **Verify the work was accomplished in accordance with that data** (§ 65.95(a)(1)) — the IA's inspection must be substantive; the FAA Chief Counsel interpretation (faa.gov/media/14341) is explicit that an approval without actual inspection is not acceptable.
6. **Confirm the IA's own capability** for this product: equipment, facilities, and inspection data on hand (§ 65.95(c)(4)).
7. **Complete the records**: § 43.9 entry, FAA Form 337 per Appendix B, and revise operating limitations/flight manual data under § 43.5 if changed.
8. **Retain** the IA's activity record — it feeds § 65.93 renewal (two major repairs/alterations per 90 days is one qualifying route).

---

## 8. Verification items to close before relying on this in a compliance document

1. **§ 43.7 paragraph text** — only the section title was captured in this retrieval. Pull the full section from eCFR to quote the major-alteration approval conditions exactly.
2. **§ 65.93 renewal criteria** — the "two major repairs or major alterations for each 90 days" line appeared as fragmentary text on the § 65.92 PDF page; confirm the full list and lettering.
3. **§ 65.95(c) vs. the 2018 renumbering** — the current eCFR text uses (a) privileges, (b) carry-the-card, (c) change of fixed base; the *eligibility* list is in § 65.95(c) per the GovInfo Part 65 compilation. Confirm which codification your citation style requires.
4. **Field-approval mechanics** — FAA Order 8900.1 governs how approved data is obtained when none exists; cite the current revision if the procedure is audited.

---

## 9. Bottom line

An IA is held only by a mechanic who meets **all five** § 65.95(c) criteria — A&P ratings current and in effect at least 3 years, at least 2 years actively engaged, a fixed base of operations, equipment/facilities/inspection data on hand, and a passing IA written test covering return to service after major repairs and major alterations. Holding that authorization is what permits the holder, under § 65.95(a)(1), to inspect and approve for return to service an aircraft or related part or appliance after a major alteration — excluding aircraft under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program, and only where the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator.
